name: websocketd
why: Exposes ordinary stdin and stdout programs as WebSockets, a charming door into a protocol nobody looks at.

brief.what_it_is: websocketd is a single command-line binary that wraps an ordinary program and serves it over a WebSocket. The program reads lines from stdin and writes lines to stdout, and websocketd turns each incoming WebSocket message into a stdin line and each stdout line into an outgoing WebSocket message. Each browser connection gets its own process, which websocketd starts on connect and stops on disconnect. It also includes a static file server, a classic CGI server, and a built-in developer console for inspecting frames.
brief.why_it_exists: The author's framing is that any program that can read stdin and write stdout can become a WebSocket server, with no networking library, framework, or change to the program. The README says 'WebSocket-capable applications can now be built very easily.'
brief.how_it_works: On startup websocketd listens on a port. When a client connects, it forks the configured program and pipes each client message to the program's stdin followed by a newline. Each newline-terminated line the program prints to stdout is sent to the client as a WebSocket message. When the socket closes, the process is shut down, and teardown signals the whole process group. The homepage describes the model as 'CGI's idea, applied to WebSockets.'

brief.install_notes: No runtime, account, or configuration is needed. Download the single executable for Linux, macOS, or Windows from the install page at websocketd.com/docs/start/install/, or use 'brew install websocketd' on a Mac. The README says there are no installers, package managers, or external libraries. The example HTML page connects to ws://localhost:8080/ and can be opened from disk with a file:// URL. I did not open the install page, so per-platform details are not verified.
brief.standout: The program stays an ordinary stdin/stdout program, with no WebSocket library and no code changes, and the same script runs unchanged in a shell. The built-in dev console lets you test the script from a browser with no client code, which is unusual for a tool at this scale.
brief.status: unknown. The homepage and GitHub README show no release date, last-commit date, or deprecation note. The README does describe recent-sounding features, including the dev console, Unix socket support, --socketmode, and --passstderr, which suggests active work, but I did not confirm this from dates.
brief.caveats: No release date or last-commit date was visible, so currency is unconfirmed. The README warns that SERVER_NAME and SERVER_PORT mirror the client's Host header and should not be used for access decisions. Teardown signals the whole process group, so scripts that deliberately spawn survivors need setsid. The README's own description is focused on Linux, macOS, and Windows, and I did not check build instructions or license terms.
quotes: Turn any program into a WebSocket server
As long as you can write an executable program that reads STDIN and writes to STDOUT, you can build a WebSocket server.
It is CGI’s idea, applied to WebSockets.
